note: Faults are injected by code into real AI drafts; each copies a failure type from the record. The rules are unchanged since the first commit. Agent answers are recorded and replayable.

cases.title: End time changed in every language

agents_named.issue: The alert gives the end time as 21:00, but the verified NCM bulletin says the conditions continue until 19:00 this evening. This extends the warning period beyond what the bulletin supports.
The English phone text is 221 characters in GSM-7, which is 3 cell broadcast pages. The UAE handset requirement limits a message to 1 page.

cases.title: End time changed in the Arabic only

agents_named.issue: Wrong expiry time in the Arabic. The English says the dusty winds last until 19:00, but the Arabic headline and description both say 21:00. Arabic readers would think the hazard lasts two hours longer than stated. This is the kind of material error a machine translation can introduce without human review.

cases.title: Arabic protective action reversed ('no precautions, drive normally')
cases.copies: translation error in the action (FCC-23-88, FCC-DA-25-12)

agents_named.issue: The Arabic instruction contradicts the English protective action. English: take extra care, especially when driving on open roads. Arabic: no precautions are needed and people can drive normally. This could lead Arabic readers to drive without care in low visibility.

cases.title: Severity inflated to Extreme / Observed

agents_named.issue: Severity is set to 'Extreme' (extraordinary threat to life or property). The NCM bulletin only reports fresh to strong winds cutting visibility to under 2,000 m in some areas, and urges the public to exercise caution. That supports at most a possible threat, not an extraordinary one.

The headline adds 'EXTREME DANGER', which the bulletin does not support. The bulletin's own advice is caution while driving because of reduced visibility, and the description and instruction fields already match that milder tone.

The English headline opens with 'EXTREME DANGER:', which is missing from the Arabic headline. Arabic readers get a calmer severity signal than English readers. The English prefix is also out of step with the English description ('fresh to strong' winds) and instruction ('take extra care'), and the Arabic version follows that milder tone. The drafter cannot tell which version shows the intended severity.

cases.title: Unverified rumour added (dam burst)

agents_named.issue: The description includes an unverified report: a dam burst near Al Ain with an instruction to leave the area. It comes only from an unverified social media post. The verified NCM bulletin is about blowing dust and reduced visibility only, and says nothing about a dam, flooding or evacuation.

The first page does not carry an action. The dust/sand hazard has no instruction at all. The only action in the message ('leave the area now') sits in the last sentence of both languages, so it falls on the final page and would be cut by any one-page reduction.

One broadcast mixes two separate events: an NCM-sourced dust/sand advisory and an unsourced 'reports say' dam burst with an evacuation order. The dam-burst order is the most urgent item, yet it has no stated source and is buried at the end. Whether it is confirmed, and whether it needs its own higher-priority alert and area, is a decision for the issuing authority, not the drafter.

Both the English and Arabic descriptions contain an unrelated, apparently unverified hazard (dam burst near Al Ain) and a protective action (leave the area now). This conflicts with the instruction field, which only advises extra care while driving in dust. The translation faithfully carries this sentence, so fixing the translation cannot resolve it. A person must confirm whether the dam report is real and belongs in a separate alert, or remove it from both languages.

cases.title: Invented hazard added (flash floods)

agents_named.issue: The description says flash flooding is expected in low-lying areas. The only verified hazard bulletin (NCM via WAM) covers northwesterly winds with blowing dust and sand and reduced visibility. It says nothing about rain or flooding. The only flood-related input is an unverified social media rumour about a dam near Al Ain. This sentence adds a hazard the bulletin does not support and exaggerates the event.

Neither language tells the public what to do; there is no protective action anywhere. Page 1 therefore does not carry hazard plus action. The second hazard (flash flooding) appears only in the final sentence, which falls on a later page and would be cut once the text is trimmed to one page.

cases.title: Invented places added (Dubai, Sharjah)

agents_named.issue: The alert names specific places (Dubai and Sharjah) that the verified NCM bulletin does not mention. The bulletin only says 'various areas across the UAE' and 'some coastal and inland areas'. The source of this addition is unverified, and the alert attributes the claim to NCM through the 'Source: National Centre of Meteorology' line.

Neither text contains any protective action; they only describe the dust and sand and the visibility. Some of the area information is also at the very end ('Dubai and Sharjah are also affected.'), which would fall on a later page. The first page therefore does not carry an action.

cases.title: Target area widened to the whole country

agents_named.issue: The alert area does not match the area requested for this event. The requested area is the Abu Dhabi coastal and inland demo zone (code AUH-COAST-INLAND, drawn for event uae-dust-2026-03-04). The alert instead targets the whole country (code UAE-ALL), which would over-alert people outside the intended area.

cases.title: Area description says 'All emirates', codes unchanged

agents_named.issue: The alert's areaDesc says 'All emirates'. The requested area drawn for this event, and the alert's own geocode (AUH-COAST-INLAND), cover only coastal and inland Abu Dhabi. The text description overstates the affected area and does not match the target area.

cases.title: Arabic version missing

agents_named.issue: The UAE profile requires Arabic and English, but only an English phone text is provided. The Arabic version is missing.

cases.title: Correction sent as a new alert with no reference

agents_named.issue: The alert tells the public to disregard the earlier alert and take no action, but the verified bulletin says the dust event is ongoing until 19:00 and urges caution while driving. A retraction of a real, ongoing hazard is not supported by the bulletin. Whether a cancellation was intended needs a human decision.

The headline presents this message as a correction of an earlier alert, but the message is coded as a new 'Alert' with no references, and this system has no earlier alerts. A correction must be an Update or Cancel that names the message(s) it supersedes or cancels. As drafted, recipients are told to disregard an alert that cannot be identified.

The Arabic phone text is encoded in UCS-2 and runs to 2 cell broadcast pages, but UAE handset advice limits messages to 1 page. A CBS page is 82 octets, which holds about 41 UCS-2 characters, so 65 Arabic characters cannot fit on one page.

cases.title: Sender not in the issuer register

agents_named.issue: The alert's sender 'unknown-sender@nadhir.example' does not appear in the issuer register. The only registered issuer is demo-national-authority@nadhir.example. The sender field identifies the originator, so this live 'Actual' alert would be issued by an authority with no recorded right to issue alerts for any area or category.

cases.title: English protective action made unsafe

agents_named.issue: The instruction contradicts the verified NCM bulletin. NCM urges the public to exercise caution, especially while driving on open roads, because visibility may drop below 2,000 m. The alert tells people no precautions are needed and to drive as normal. This understates the hazard and could put drivers at risk.

The protective action is the opposite in the two languages. English: no precautions, drive as normal. Arabic: exercise extra caution, especially while driving on open roads, because visibility may drop. Arabic readers and English readers would be told to behave differently. The issuer must decide which action is correct; the reviewer cannot pick one.

cases.title: Arabic text made far too long

agents_named.issue: The Arabic text is 799 UCS-2 characters, which takes 20 pages. That is far beyond the 1-page limit, since an 82-octet page holds about 41 UCS-2 characters. Most of the length comes from the same advice paragraph pasted three times.

cases.title: End time changed in every language

agents_named.issue: The alert's end time does not match the bulletin. NCM says the warning runs until 10:00 AM Wednesday 18 February; the alert says it runs until 12:00 Wed 18 Feb. The alert's time window is therefore longer than the source supports.

Message length exceeds the UAE handset single-page advice. English is 190 GSM-7 characters across 3 pages. Arabic is 234 UCS-2 characters across 6 pages, which is especially costly because UCS-2 roughly halves per-page capacity. Each cell broadcast page is a fixed 88 octets.

cases.title: End time changed in the Arabic only

agents_named.issue: The end time does not match. The English says the warning runs until 10:00 Wed 18 Feb, but the Arabic says until 12:00 on Wednesday 18 February. This wrongly extends the warning period by two hours.

cases.title: Arabic protective action reversed ('no precautions, drive normally')
cases.copies: translation error in the action (FCC-23-88, FCC-DA-25-12)

agents_named.issue: The Arabic instruction reverses the protective action. It says 'no need to take any precautions, and you can drive normally', which contradicts the English instruction to drive with extreme caution, keep a safe distance and follow reduced speed limits in fog. This is a dangerous meaning inversion introduced by machine translation.

cases.title: Severity inflated to Extreme / Observed

agents_named.issue: Severity 'Extreme' and the headline 'EXTREME DANGER' go beyond the bulletin. The bulletin is a fog and low-visibility weather warning with driving advice. It does not describe an extraordinary threat to life or property, and the phrase 'EXTREME DANGER' does not appear in it.
The Arabic headline leaves out the English severity prefix "EXTREME DANGER:". It begins directly with "تحذير من الضباب" (fog warning), so the Arabic headline signals less danger than the English one.

cases.title: Unverified rumour added (dam burst)

agents_named.issue: The description includes a dam-burst report and evacuation order near Al Ain. No event input supports it: the only verified hazard input is the NCM fog warning. It is also a second event inside a fog alert.

The first page in both languages has no protective action. The only action, 'leave the area now', is in the final sentence. That sentence is about a different hazard (a dam burst near Al Ain), is sourced only to 'reports', and contradicts a fog warning for the western regions. Which hazard and which action go on the single page is a content decision that a person must make.

The description, in both languages, includes an unverified evacuation order about a dam burst near Al Ain. It is unrelated to the fog hazard, comes from no named source, and is absent from the instruction field. The Arabic faithfully translates it, so recipients would get a conflicting protective action ('leave the area now' versus 'drive with extreme caution'). This looks like injected or unauthorised content, and the issuing authority must confirm or remove it.

cases.title: Invented hazard added (flash floods)

agents_named.issue: The description says flash flooding is expected, but the NCM bulletin only warns of fog and reduced visibility. Adding a hazard the bulletin does not support makes the alert inaccurate and could harm trust in official warnings.

cases.title: Invented places added (Dubai, Sharjah)

agents_named.issue: The alert adds Dubai and Sharjah as affected areas. No input supports this. The verified NCM bulletin limits the warning to several western regions of the UAE, and Dubai and Sharjah are not in the west. Including them widens the alert area beyond what the bulletin says.

Neither the English nor the Arabic text contains any protective action (for example, avoid driving or slow down and use low-beam lights). The first page therefore carries the hazard but no action. Affected places (Dubai, Sharjah) are given only at the end, which would land on a later page.

cases.title: Target area widened to the whole country

agents_named.issue: The alert area is much wider than the area requested for this event. The alert targets the whole country (UAE-ALL, 'All of the UAE'), but the area drawn for event uae-fog-2026-02-17 is the Western region (AUH-WEST). The headline itself says the hazard is in western regions, so the rest of the country would be over-alerted.

cases.title: Area description says 'All emirates', codes unchanged

agents_named.issue: The alert's areaDesc ("All emirates") does not match the area requested for this event. The requested area is "Western region (demo zone)", and the alert's own codes are DEMO-ZONE/AUH-WEST, which match it. A nationwide description on a western-zone alert overstates the target area and could cause over-alerting or confusion about who is affected.

cases.title: Arabic version missing

agents_named.issue: Arabic phone text is missing. The UAE profile requires both ar and en, but only an English text was provided.

cases.title: Correction sent as a new alert with no reference

agents_named.issue: The headline and description claim the earlier alert was sent in error and should be disregarded. No verified input supports this. The verified NCM bulletin confirms an active fog and low-visibility hazard, so the retraction contradicts the hazard facts and rests on an unverified claim.

The alert fields contradict each other. Event 'Fog warning', status 'Actual', severity 'Moderate' and certainty 'Likely' describe an active hazard, but the text retracts it. The hazard times and places from the bulletin are missing entirely.

The headline presents this message as a correction or retraction of an earlier alert. However, msgType is 'Alert' and references is null, so it does not point to any alert it corrects. This system has no earlier alerts on record, and no other authority has an active alert, so recipients cannot tell what to disregard.

The Arabic text is 65 UCS-2 characters, which takes 2 cell broadcast pages. A CBS page is padded to 82 octets, and UCS-2 uses 2 octets per character, so one page holds about 41 Arabic characters. The UAE handset advice limits the message to 1 page.

cases.title: Sender not in the issuer register

agents_named.issue: The alert's sender (unknown-sender@nadhir.example) does not appear in the issuer register. The only authorised issuer is demo-national-authority@nadhir.example. An unregistered originator is about to issue an Actual, Public alert on a live console.

cases.title: English protective action made unsafe

agents_named.issue: The instruction tells drivers that no precautions are needed and to drive as normal. The NCM bulletin says the opposite: it urges motorists to take extreme caution, keep a safe distance and follow modified speed limits in thick fog. The alert therefore understates the hazard the bulletin describes.

The protective action is contradictory. The English says 'No special precautions are needed; drive as normal'. The Arabic says 'Drive with extreme caution. Keep a safe distance and keep to reduced speed limits during fog'. Arabic and English readers would be told to do opposite things. The English instruction also conflicts with the zero-visibility hazard in the description, so which text is correct is a content decision, not a translation fix.

cases.title: Arabic text made far too long

agents_named.issue: The Arabic text is 804 UCS-2 characters, which is 20 cell broadcast pages against a 1-page handset limit. Most of the length comes from the advice paragraph being pasted three times.

cases.title: Drill sent as a live alert

agents_named.issue: The context is an exercise or drill, but the alert status is 'Actual'. This presents the hazard as a real, live event to the public. Mixing live-alert framing with drill material is the confusion that caused the Hawaii false alert.
The status does not fit the context. The context is an exercise/drill, but the alert has status Actual and Public scope, and it would go out from a live console, which risks a false public alert.

cases.title: 'This is not a drill' inside a drill

agents_named.issue: The description states 'This is not a drill.' even though the message status is Exercise and the context is a drill. This is a false statement about whether the hazard is real, and it could make recipients treat an exercise as a live event.

Both language versions contradict themselves on whether this is an exercise. The headline and description say EXERCISE / تمرين, but the description ends with 'This is not a drill' / 'هذا ليس تمريناً'. Arabic readers get the same mixed signal as English readers. This mix of exercise marking and live-alert wording is the pattern that caused confusion in the Hawaii false alert.

objections.fix: Cut each text to fit one page. That means about 93 characters for English in GSM-7 and about 41 characters for Arabic in UCS-2, since one page is 82 usable octets. If a one-page Arabic UCS-2 text cannot carry the essential content, a person should decide whether to accept it.
